co_central_quarry_wall.blurb: Central Quarry Wall is a short run of eleven routes in the middle of the tall main face of the Quarry Wall complex, in Unaweep Canyon not far from Grand Junction. Almost everything here is traditional crack and face climbing, with a single aid line, and the difficulty sits in the upper-intermediate to advanced range: a few lines around 5.10, a handful at 5.11 and a few at 5.12. Many routes can be broken into two pitches or run together as one long pitch. The face catches the morning sun, which makes it a better summer choice than an afternoon one. Expect a serious, committing day on a wall that rewards a full trad rack.

co_front_porch_the.blurb: The Front Porch is a small cliff in the Narrows corridor south of Carbondale, and it is the one nearest the road, so the walk in is short. It holds eleven routes, nearly all of them bolted sport climbs plus a lone trad line. The grades start easy but cluster at the harder end of the range, with most lines in the 5.10 to 5.11 band, so it suits climbers comfortable on steep, sustained pitches. The face takes the morning sun and dries quickly after rain, and the climbing is regarded as some of the best rock in the Narrows. Wear a helmet, since the broader canyon can be loose.

co_gargoyle_wall_the.blurb: The Gargoyle Wall is a small cliff within Castlewood Canyon State Park, the creek-cut canyon on the plains southeast of Denver. Eleven routes are recorded: six top-rope lines, three sport routes and two trad lines. It leans toward difficulty, with five of the climbs at 5.12, a few at 5.10 and 5.11, and just one in the 5.9 range, so it is not the place for a first outing. The wall sees fewer visitors than most of the park because it sits at the end of one of the longer walks in the canyon, which usually means quieter climbing.

co_joe_97_boulder.blurb: Joe 97 is a single boulder in the Main Area of the Lunch Loop bouldering zone near Grand Junction, a short stroll up the first trail on the right from the trailhead lot. The boulder carries its name in spray paint. It holds eleven problems spread across the whole range from V0 up to V6, with the bulk between V1 and V4 and a couple of hard lines at the top. That spread makes it a good stop for a mixed group. Bring a crash pad, as there is little else to cushion falls, and plan to walk off after topping out.

co_hemingway_wall.blurb: Hemingway Wall is a cliff on the Meadow Dome in Staunton State Park, in the foothills southwest of Denver. It carries eleven routes, a fairly even split between sport and traditional lines, and the grades are friendly: mostly 5.7 to 5.9, with a couple of 5.10s. The lines run long, some are multi-pitch, and a few call for two ropes to get down, so it is more of a day on a real wall than a quick crag session. Reach it by walking to the foot of the dome and turning right. It suits climbers stepping up to longer moderate routes.

co_friends_and_family_wall.blurb: Friends and Family Wall is the lowest tier of the Redstein formation near Redstone, in the Carbondale area. It is a gentle, welcoming slab of long, closely spaced, moderate sport routes, each about one pitch and 80 to 90 feet. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.10, so it is a strong choice for newer leaders and for groups with mixed ability. The surface is textured with embedded pebbles and cobbles, some of them slippery, and there is a fair amount of loose rock, so a helmet is wise. The base gets plenty of sun, which makes spring, fall or evenings the comfortable times to visit.
